objective.title: Approach optimal play through robust self-play
objective.summary: The long-term goal is approximate optimal / equilibrium-oriented play in the closed-team-sheet VGC game. Measure progress across held-out teams and a varied opponent set; report average, lower-percentile, and worst-case results. No single opponent or fixed win-rate threshold defines completion.

candidate.label: Current in-battle policy vs Round424 start
candidate.status: Current validated candidate · Round436 ablation and external screens inconclusive
candidate.note: Round431 scored 49.36% [45.85%, 52.93%] against Round430, and Round432 scored 47.90% [44.29%, 51.61%]; neither showed a clear gain. Round430 remains the validated in-battle candidate. Round402's 77.15% result is a separate team-preview selector benchmark. Round432 external screens also showed no clear lift: all paired 95% intervals vs Round430 and Round431 include zero. Round432 cross-opponent equal-weight mean/median/p10/worst were 60.35%/48.83%/47.64%/47.46%; the mean is buoyed by random play. Round435 used a Round434 restricted-game mixture (31.7% Round430 / 68.3% Round432 in the policy pool) and scored 52.98% [49.41%, 56.59%] head-to-head with Round430; all matched external deltas vs Round430/432 included zero. Round430 remains the candidate. Round436 removed hidden-set auxiliary loss on the identical Round435 data; it scored 53.42% [49.80%, 56.93%] vs Round435 over 512 clusters (one incomplete game), an inconclusive ablation. Round430 remains the validated candidate. Round436 external screens at 256 clusters found no supported paired gain vs Round435: deltas on 128 shared clusters were +0.20 pp vs Max Damage [-0.59,+0.98], +0.39 pp vs public Counterplay [-0.59,+1.37], 0.00 pp vs random [-0.78,+0.78], and -0.20 pp vs Round102 [-0.98,+0.39]. Round436 remains unpromoted; Round430 is still the validated candidate.

speed.context: Round430 20,000-game complete training iteration including rollout and PPO preparation/optimization; Round435 full aggregate rollout telemetry was not captured. Not raw simulator speed.
speed.decision_latency: ~85 ms action selection per policy-pool match
speed.current_bottleneck: Round435 shard profile: policy inference 65–73 ms/match vs historical policies; public counterplay scoring about 76 ms/match; observation encoding 25–28 ms; Showdown roundtrip 28–37 ms. PPO audit/record preparation plus tensor aggregation took 159.3 s for 20,000 games versus about 55 s optimization. Full aggregate Round435 rollout rate was not captured.
speed.gpu_status: RTX 4060 used for PPO optimization; rollout inference and Showdown simulation remain CPU-side
speed.profile_context: Round430 remains the latest complete end-to-end 20,000-game profile: eight-worker rollout 22.55 games/s and full iteration 16.49 games/s. Round435 offers newer per-shard timings but no valid aggregate rate after preflight recovery. Per-opponent shard rates are not aggregate rates. Action selection contains policy inference; Public Counterplay scoring is nested inside action selection.

active_training_profile.status: Round435 per-worker profile · Round430 retained as candidate
active_training_profile.context: Round435 single-shard timing samples from 20,000-game PPO update, after seat-balanced recovery from one duplicate-team record. The wrapper did not capture full-run aggregate rollout telemetry. Do not sum per-shard rates as aggregate.
active_training_profile.finding: Round435 measured about 76 ms/match of Public Counterplay scoring, 65–73 ms/match policy inference against pool opponents, and 28–37 ms/match Showdown engine time. PPO record preparation plus tensor aggregation took 159.3 s for 20,000 games, versus about 55 s optimization. Improve automatic duplicate-team recovery, then prioritize batched policy inference and audited record parsing/tensor preparation.

opportunities.title: 1 · Batch policy inference across live rollouts
opportunities.detail: Historical-policy rollouts spent about 72 ms/match in inference. Workers currently infer independently on CPU. Gather ready decisions from concurrent matches into a shared batch, then compare CPU batching with a single GPU inference service at observed batch sizes. Measure games/s, queue delay, and p95 decision latency before adopting it.

opportunities.title: 2 · Reduce observation encoding work
opportunities.detail: Encoding used about 22–29 ms/match. Precompute static dex/team features, cache repeated derived values, and reuse compact numeric buffers across decisions. Profile each stage and retain the closed-team-sheet leakage audit.

opportunities.title: 3 · Batch rollouts and tune worker count
opportunities.detail: A fixed 240-game Max Damage benchmark measured 30.94 games/s at 8 workers, versus 29.09 at 12 and 26.04 at 16; memory also rose from 6.77 GB at 8 to 13.25 GB at 16. Keep 8 as the measured setting for now. Test batching requests across those workers before increasing concurrency.

opportunities.title: 4 · Reduce counterplay scorer cost
opportunities.detail: A per-decision cache for repeated public damage calculations cut scorer time from 203.4 to 62.6 ms/match (69%) in a paired 32-game single-worker probe. In a separate 240-game, 8-worker run, scoring averaged 80.1 ms/match and aggregate rollout throughput was 23.51 games/s, with no timeouts or corrections. Still compare an 8-worker pre-cache control and rerun the full mixed PPO iteration; then profile repeated speed and legality calculations.

opportunities.title: 5 · Accelerate audited PPO record preparation
opportunities.detail: Round431 spent 153.2 s parsing and preparing rollout records for a 20,000-game update, then 6.2 s aggregating tensors and 51.0 s optimizing. Profile JSON decoding and perspective/feature reconstruction; benchmark compact buffered or columnar chunks while keeping the same 20,000-game audit, closed-sheet leakage checks, and replayed tensors.

opportunities.title: 6 · Trim trajectory persistence
opportunities.detail: Writes used 7–12 ms/match and Round424 stored about 1.8 GB for 10,000 games. Benchmark buffered compact records or chunk compression after the higher-cost action and inference paths.

speed.jax_decision: Round430 confirms the Showdown engine used about 18% of policy-pool match time and 8% against Public Counterplay; a simulator-only port would leave the larger measured policy, observation, and baseline-scoring costs intact. Keep Showdown as the correctness reference and require an end-to-end measured gain before a JAX/GPU engine prototype.
speed.remaining_summary: For the historical-policy pool, Showdown used about 34 ms of 193.5 ms per match (~17.5%); the remaining ~82.5% is about 159.6 ms: 84.8 ms action selection (53% of the remainder, including 73.1 ms inference), 27.4 ms observation encoding (17%), 12.6 ms trajectory writes (8%), about 10.5 ms setup (7%), 2 ms preview/first step (1%), and about 22.3 ms other overhead (14%). For Public Counterplay, the engine used about 28 ms of 359.5 ms (~8%); its scorer alone used 239 ms (67%).

remaining_components.note: Includes 73.1 ms policy inference; do not add inference again.

speed.worker_scaling_context: Round430 CPU rollout scaling on the 16-logical-CPU host, with 240 complete matches per setting against Max Damage. Eight workers were fastest in this short single-opponent sample; 12 and 16 workers consumed more memory and ran slower. Test batching across the existing workers before increasing worker count.

policy_inference_benchmark.context: Round430 checkpoint on 256 perspective-safe rollout states; 1 CPU thread, 5 warmups, 30 timed repeats. Timings include host-to-device transfer and action/value synchronization; collation is reported separately. Queue wait is excluded.
policy_inference_benchmark.interpretation: CUDA is slower for single states and roughly tied with CPU at batch 8, about 51% faster at batch 16, and 2.6x faster at batch 32. Queue wait is excluded. A scalar-clamp optimization reduced warm native action-feature time 41.3% (0.1983 to 0.1165 ms/state) with exact outputs against the prior NumPy-clamp implementation on 256 inputs; whole-match speed impact is not yet measured.
policy_inference_benchmark.feature_replay_caveat: The initial Round430 parity audit used initial-team opponent ordering and PPO's conditionally narrowed action mask, unlike live feature generation. New rollout data now saves per-step opponent preview order, the raw feature mask, the PPO conditional mask, and encoder version. On a fresh 64-game rollout (128 perspective records, 481 feature states), recomputation matched every saved feature value exactly. Legacy Round430 records remain missing the raw action mask, but PPO continues to train from the saved feature arrays.

counterplay_cache_benchmark.context: Same Round430 checkpoint, VGC format, 32 episode seeds, one CPU worker, and /dev/null trajectory output before and after memoizing repeated deterministic damage estimates within each joint-action score. This is a microbenchmark, not the standard 8-worker mixed-training run.
counterplay_cache_benchmark.result: Both runs produced 13 Headless P1 wins and 19 Headless P2 wins, with 0 timeouts and 0 action corrections. Policy inference averaged 31.9 vs 31.4 ms/match, observation encoding 19.5 vs 19.1 ms, and engine roundtrips 29.2 vs 28.1 ms.
counterplay_cache_benchmark.limitation: The 32-game before/after is paired on identical seeds. The 8-worker rollout validates concurrent operation but has no pre-cache 8-worker control; full 20,000-game mixed PPO throughput has not yet been remeasured.

latest_run.summary: Round436 removed hidden-set auxiliary loss from a same-data PPO ablation and was then screened against four held-out opponents at 256 clusters each. Paired deltas vs Round435 on 128 shared clusters all had 95% intervals covering zero; Round430 remains the validated candidate.
latest_run.evaluation: No supported paired gain vs Round435 across Max Damage, public counterplay, random, and Round102

method: Native self-play PPO for in-battle decisions. Terminal win/loss remains the main objective; win-probability and hidden-set prediction are auxiliary tasks. Search comes after a stronger policy.
jax_decision: Round430 has a confirmed self-play head-to-head lift over Round424, but external-opponent screens remain inconclusive. Prioritize measured inference batching, observation throughput, and rollouts; keep equilibrium-oriented opponent coverage and defer a JAX/GPU engine rewrite until its end-to-end payoff is measured.
evaluation_note: Score rates include wins and half credit for draws. Use paired held-out teams, side swaps, repeated outcomes, and cluster intervals. Track results across public counterplay, random, historical PPO, and Max Damage; no one matchup percentage is the finish line. Round431's equal-weight four-opponent mean was 59.86%, but the median was 48.05%, p10 47.30%, and worst score 47.07%; the mean is lifted by random play. All paired differences vs Round430 included zero.
